Use the photograph to answer the question.

This photograph, titled 'Into the Jaws of Death,' was taken on June 6, 1944, by Chief Photographer's Mate Robert F. Sargent of the U.S. Coast Guard. The image shows American soldiers wading through waist-deep water from an LCVP (Landing Craft, Vehicle, Personnel) toward a beach. The view is from inside the landing craft, looking out toward the shore. Soldiers are visible from behind as they move through the water toward the French coastline.

(Photograph by Chief Photographer's Mate Robert F. Sargent, U.S. Coast Guard, June 6, 1944. National Archives and Records Administration.)

Which event and location are shown in this photograph?

choices.text: The Battle of Iwo Jima in the Pacific Ocean, February 1945
The Allied evacuation at Dunkirk, France, May–June 1940
The Allied landings in North Africa during Operation Torch, November 1942
The D-Day Allied invasion of Normandy, France, June 6, 1944

items.explanation: The photograph documents the D-Day landings on June 6, 1944, at Normandy, France — specifically the assault at Omaha Beach, where American troops stormed ashore as part of Operation Overlord, the Allied invasion of Nazi-occupied Western Europe. The image is one of the most iconic photographs of World War II. Choice A identifies a different Pacific Theater battle. Choice B names a different European theater event. Choice C describes a different North African campaign.

What was the strategic significance of the Allied invasion of Normandy shown in this photograph?

choices.text: It opened a Western Front that forced Germany to fight on two major fronts, overstretching German military resources
It was necessary to stop a German offensive that was on the verge of defeating the Soviet Union
It was designed primarily to gain Allied control of the Atlantic Ocean and cut off German supply ships
It was intended to allow the United States to capture German nuclear research facilities before the Soviet Union could reach them

items.explanation: Operation Overlord opened a major Allied front in Western Europe, forcing Germany to fight on two major fronts simultaneously — against the advancing Soviets in the East and the Allied forces pushing through France in the West. This two-front pressure critically overstretched German military resources and accelerated the collapse of Nazi Germany. Choice B is incorrect because Germany was not close to surrendering before D-Day. Choice C misdescribes the purpose — D-Day was a ground invasion, not aimed at naval control. Choice D describes an irrelevant strategic objective.

Analyze why the Allied invasion of Normandy on June 6, 1944, is considered a major turning point in World War II in Europe.

choices.text: D-Day succeeded primarily because German forces had already been weakened beyond recovery by Allied strategic bombing of German cities
D-Day was the first major Allied victory of the war and reversed a series of continuous Allied defeats on all fronts
D-Day established an irreversible Allied foothold in Western Europe, creating two-front pressure that made Germany's military position untenable and accelerated its defeat
D-Day was decisive primarily because it secured Allied control of the English Channel, cutting off all German supply lines to France

items.explanation: D-Day marked a decisive shift in the war's momentum because it established a permanent Allied foothold on Western Europe's mainland that could not be repelled, committed massive Allied forces to a direct drive toward Germany, and created the two-front pressure that made Nazi Germany's strategic position untenable. Within a year, Germany surrendered. The invasion proved that a large-scale amphibious assault against German-held Europe was achievable, fundamentally changing the trajectory of the war. Choice A attributes the turning point to an incorrect cause. Choice B mistakes timing — the Soviet victory at Stalingrad in 1943 is often cited as an earlier turning point on the Eastern Front. Choice D misidentifies a logistical factor as the decisive strategic element.

items.stem:
Read the following excerpt from Justice Robert Jackson's dissent in Korematsu v. United States, 323 U.S. 214 (1944) (Supreme Court of the United States, public domain):

"A military order, however unconstitutional, is not apt to last longer than the military emergency. Even during that period a succeeding commander may revoke it all. But once a judicial opinion rationalizes such an order to show that it conforms to the Constitution... the Court for all time has validated the principle of racial discrimination in criminal procedure and of transplanting American citizens. The principle then lies about like a loaded weapon ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of an urgent need."

Using this dissent and your knowledge of Japanese American internment, write a CER response that evaluates the constitutional and human rights implications of Executive Order 9066 and the Supreme Court's Korematsu ruling. Your response must: (1) analyze the specific conditions and government actions that led to internment; (2) evaluate Jackson's 'loaded weapon' argument and what it predicted about future civil liberties; (3) assess the legacy of internment, including the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (reparations) and how Korematsu has been invoked in later civil liberties cases. Synthesize constitutional, human rights, and historical dimensions.
items.stemEs:
Lee el siguiente fragmento del voto disidente del Juez Robert Jackson en Korematsu v. Estados Unidos, 323 U.S. 214 (1944) (Tribunal Supremo de los Estados Unidos, dominio público):

"Una orden militar, aunque sea inconstitucional, no es probable que dure más que la emergencia militar. Incluso durante ese período, un comandante sucesor puede revocarla. Pero una vez que una opinión judicial racionaliza dicha orden para mostrar que se ajusta a la Constitución... el Tribunal ha validado para todos los tiempos el principio de la discriminación racial en el procedimiento penal y del trasplante de ciudadanos americanos. El principio entonces yace como un arma cargada lista para la mano de cualquier autoridad que pueda presentar una afirmación plausible de una necesidad urgente."

Usando este voto disidente y tu conocimiento del internamiento de japoneses americanos, escribe una respuesta CER que evalúe las implicaciones constitucionales y de derechos humanos de la Orden Ejecutiva 9066 y el fallo Korematsu de la Corte Suprema. Tu respuesta debe: (1) analizar las condiciones específicas y las acciones gubernamentales que llevaron al internamiento; (2) evaluar el argumento del 'arma cargada' de Jackson y lo que predijo sobre futuras libertades civiles; (3) evaluar el legado del internamiento, incluida la Ley de Libertades Civiles de 1988 (reparaciones) y cómo Korematsu ha sido invocado en casos posteriores de libertades civiles. Sintetiza dimensiones constitucionales, de derechos humanos e históricas.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score response will: (1) Claim: Executive Order 9066 and the Supreme Court's Korematsu ruling represent a profound constitutional failure that validated racial discrimination under the guise of military necessity, and Jackson's dissent proved prophetic as the precedent has been cited in later civil liberties conflicts. (2) Evidence: EO 9066 (February 19, 1942) — authorized internment; 120,000 Japanese Americans (70,000 U.S. citizens) relocated; War Relocation Authority camps (Manzanar, Topaz, others); Korematsu decision (6-3, December 1944) — upheld internment; Murphy, Jackson, and Roberts dissents; Civil Liberties Act of 1988 — $20,000 reparations per surviving internee, government apology; Korematsu formally overruled in Trump v. Hawaii (2018) — but that case itself raised Jackson's 'loaded weapon' concern anew. (3) Reasoning: Jackson's dissent predicted that judicial validation of racial exclusion creates a constitutional precedent that can be revived by future governments. The Civil Liberties Act (1988) was the government's acknowledgment that the internment was a product of 'racial prejudice, wartime hysteria, and a failure of political leadership.' The Korematsu ruling's long shadow demonstrates how wartime emergency powers, once judicially approved, persist as threats to civil liberties.

items.stem:
Analyze the following two primary source excerpts and construct a document-based argument about the constitutional crisis created by Japanese American internment.

DOCUMENT A: Excerpt from Executive Order 9066, issued by President Franklin D. Roosevelt, February 19, 1942 (Federal Register, 1942; National Archives, public domain):
"I hereby authorize and direct the Secretary of War, and the Military Commanders whom he may from time to time designate, whenever he or any designated Commander deems such action necessary or desirable, to prescribe military areas in such places and of such extent as he or the appropriate Military Commander may determine, from which any or all persons may be excluded..."

DOCUMENT B: Excerpt from Justice Robert Jackson's dissent in Korematsu v. United States, 323 U.S. 214 (1944) (Supreme Court of the United States, public domain):
"But once a judicial opinion rationalizes such an order to show that it conforms to the Constitution, or rather rationalizes the Constitution to show that the Constitution sanctions such an order, the Court for all time has validated the principle of racial discrimination in criminal procedure... The principle then lies about like a loaded weapon ready for the hand of any authority that can bring forward a plausible claim of an urgent need."

Using HIPP analysis for each document and your knowledge of Japanese American internment, construct an argument evaluating: (1) what EO 9066 reveals about the limits of civil liberties in wartime; (2) how Jackson's dissent predicted future abuses of emergency power; (3) the long-term legacy of the Korematsu ruling. Include at least two pieces of outside evidence, including one from after 1945.
items.stemEs:
Analiza los siguientes dos extractos de fuentes primarias y construye un argumento basado en documentos sobre la crisis constitucional creada por el internamiento de japoneses americanos.

DOCUMENTO A: Extracto de la Orden Ejecutiva 9066, emitida por el presidente Franklin D. Roosevelt, 19 de febrero de 1942 (Registro Federal, 1942; Archivo Nacional, dominio público):
"Por la presente autorizo y dirijo al Secretario de Guerra, y a los Comandantes Militares que él pueda designar de vez en cuando, siempre que él o cualquier Comandante designado considere tal acción necesaria o deseable, a prescribir áreas militares en los lugares y de la extensión que él o el Comandante Militar apropiado puedan determinar, de las cuales cualquiera o todas las personas pueden ser excluidas..."

DOCUMENTO B: Extracto del voto disidente del Juez Robert Jackson en Korematsu v. Estados Unidos, 323 U.S. 214 (1944) (Tribunal Supremo de los Estados Unidos, dominio público):
"Pero una vez que una opinión judicial racionaliza dicha orden para mostrar que se ajusta a la Constitución, o más bien racionaliza la Constitución para mostrar que la Constitución sanciona dicha orden, el Tribunal ha validado para todos los tiempos el principio de la discriminación racial en el procedimiento penal... El principio entonces yace como un arma cargada lista para la mano de cualquier autoridad que pueda presentar una afirmación plausible de una necesidad urgente."

Usando el análisis HIPP para cada documento y tu conocimiento del internamiento de japoneses americanos, construye un argumento que evalúe: (1) qué revela la Orden Ejecutiva 9066 sobre los límites de las libertades civiles en tiempos de guerra; (2) cómo el voto disidente de Jackson predijo futuros abusos del poder de emergencia; (3) el legado a largo plazo del fallo Korematsu. Incluye al menos dos piezas de evidencia externa, incluyendo una posterior a 1945.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (6/6) response will: THESIS: E.g., 'Executive Order 9066 and the Korematsu ruling represent one of the most consequential constitutional failures of the twentieth century: by validating racial exclusion under the guise of military necessity, the Supreme Court created a precedent that — as Jackson predicted — has repeatedly threatened civil liberties in subsequent national security crises, demonstrating that constitutional rights are most fragile precisely when they are most needed.' HIPP — Doc A: Context: weeks after Pearl Harbor, wartime fear and anti-Japanese racism; Audience: Secretary of War and military commanders; Purpose: grant executive authority for civilian exclusion from military areas (deliberately vague language avoids naming race); POV: FDR prioritizing military security over civil liberties, under pressure from West Coast politicians. HIPP — Doc B: Context: wartime Supreme Court, 1944, war still ongoing; Audience: legal community, future judges; Purpose: warn that judicial validation of racial discrimination creates permanent constitutional risk; POV: Jackson as dissenter — unusually prophetic about long-term constitutional consequences. OUTSIDE EVIDENCE: 120,000 Japanese Americans interned (70,000 U.S. citizens); Manzanar, Topaz camps; Civil Liberties Act of 1988 ($20,000 reparations, government apology); Trump v. Hawaii (2018) — formally overruled Korematsu but upheld travel ban — Jackson's 'loaded weapon' argument made newly relevant. SYNTHESIS: Doc A's deliberately vague language enabled Doc B's nightmare scenario — a court that had to rationalize racial exclusion rather than reject it. The 1988 Act and 2018 case together confirm that Jackson's dissent was historically vindicated.

6 - Ejemplar: Tesis sofisticada sobre el fracaso constitucional y la profecía de Jackson. Síntesis de cómo el Doc A habilitó la preocupación del Doc B.
5 - Avanzado: Tesis clara. Ambos documentos con HIPP mayormente completo. Evidencia posterior a 1945 presente. La profecía de Jackson conectada con casos posteriores.
4 - Competente: Tesis clara. Ambos documentos con tres o más elementos HIPP. Una pieza de evidencia posterior a 1945. Análisis constitucional presente.

EXPECTATIVAS DE ANÁLISIS DE DOCUMENTOS: Orden Ejecutiva 9066 — evita deliberadamente nombrar a los japoneses americanos; esta evasión racial en el lenguaje legal es históricamente significativa. Voto disidente de Jackson — la metáfora del 'arma cargada' debe analizarse como profecía legal, no solo como protesta.

items.stem:
Using your knowledge of Japanese American internment (US.54) and the development and use of atomic weapons (US.55), write an extended response using the CER framework (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning) that addresses the following question:

Both Executive Order 9066 (Japanese American internment) and the decision to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki involved government decisions that caused severe harm to civilian populations in the name of national security. To what extent do these two decisions reflect a shared logic of 'total war' — in which the line between military necessity and the violation of individual rights or civilian lives becomes permissible — and what do they reveal about the limits of American democratic values under wartime pressure?

Your response must: (1) Advance a clear claim about the relationship between total war logic and the suspension of democratic values as illustrated by these two decisions; (2) Provide specific evidence from Executive Order 9066, the Korematsu v. United States decision (1944), the Manhattan Project, and the August 1945 atomic bombings; (3) Reason through the moral and constitutional legacy of both decisions — including the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (which formally apologized for internment) and ongoing debates about the atomic bombings' justification. Synthesize across US.54 and US.55.
items.stemEs:
Usando tu conocimiento del internamiento de japoneses-americanos (US.54) y el desarrollo y uso de armas atómicas (US.55), escribe una respuesta extendida usando el marco CER que aborde la siguiente pregunta:

Tanto la Orden Ejecutiva 9066 (internamiento de japoneses-americanos) como la decisión de lanzar bombas atómicas sobre Hiroshima y Nagasaki implicaron decisiones gubernamentales que causaron daño severo a poblaciones civiles en nombre de la seguridad nacional. ¿En qué medida estas dos decisiones reflejan una lógica compartida de 'guerra total' — en la que la línea entre la necesidad militar y la violación de los derechos individuales o las vidas civiles se vuelve permisible — y qué revelan sobre los límites de los valores democráticos estadounidenses bajo la presión de la guerra?

Tu respuesta debe: (1) Plantear una afirmación clara sobre la relación entre la lógica de la guerra total y la suspensión de los valores democráticos; (2) Proporcionar evidencia específica de la Orden Ejecutiva 9066, la decisión Korematsu v. Estados Unidos (1944), el Proyecto Manhattan y los bombardeos atómicos de agosto de 1945; (3) Razonar sobre el legado moral y constitucional de ambas decisiones. Sintetiza entre US.54 y US.55.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score response will: CLAIM — A defensible thesis connecting both decisions through a 'total war logic' framework: e.g., 'Both Executive Order 9066 and the decision to use atomic weapons reflect the logic of total war, in which military necessity was used to justify the suspension of constitutional rights and the targeting of civilian populations — revealing that American democracy is capable of profound moral failures under wartime pressure.' EVIDENCE — Internment: EO 9066 (February 19, 1942) signed by FDR; 120,000 Japanese Americans (70,000 U.S. citizens) relocated; Korematsu v. United States (1944) — Supreme Court 6-3 upheld internment (Korematsu overturned in Trump v. Hawaii 2018 by Chief Justice Roberts as 'gravely wrong'); Civil Liberties Act of 1988 — Congress apologized and paid $20,000 reparations per survivor. Atomic bombs: Manhattan Project (1942-1945), Trinity test (July 16, 1945); Hiroshima (August 6) — 80,000+ immediate deaths; Nagasaki (August 9) — 40,000+ immediate deaths; Japan surrendered August 15. Justification debate: invasion casualty projections vs. targeting civilian populations in violation of customary war law. REASONING — Both decisions were made by the same administration using the same logic: the magnitude of the threat justified the harm to civilians. Both have been subsequently judged — one (internment) as definitively wrong; the other (atomic bombs) as still contested. This asymmetry in how history has judged the two decisions is itself analytically significant.
